title: The Role of Schools Was Never the Problem
author: Stephanie Dehghani
summary: This article argues against the growing educational discourse that repositions schools as primary providers of mental health support and therapeutic intervention. The author, who has worked in both underprivileged schools and curriculum leadership, insists that the framing of schools as 'community health hubs' subtly deprioritizes the one thing schools are uniquely positioned to do: teach children to read and learn. The piece draws on the Grattan Institute's 2024 Reading Guarantee report, which found one in three Australian children cannot read proficiently — largely because of ineffective teaching approaches like whole-language and balanced literacy. The author is careful not to argue against schools partnering with health services but against the 'wellbeing drift' that treats teaching as a secondary priority to emotional regulation. The core claim is that teaching children well is itself a profound act of care, and that the evidence overwhelmingly shows literacy and academic achievement are the interventions most likely to change life trajectories for disadvantaged children.
points: The growing reframing of schools as community health hubs risks quietly deprioritizing the one thing schools are uniquely positioned to do — teach children to read and learn effectively.

The Grattan Institute's 2024 Reading Guarantee found that in a typical Australian classroom of 24 students, eight cannot read proficiently — largely because they have not been taught using evidence-based methods.

The 'wellbeing drift' in education discourse treats teaching as secondary to emotional regulation and therapeutic support, when the evidence actually shows that effective teaching is itself the most powerful intervention for disadvantaged children's life trajectories.

Schools partnering with health and allied services is entirely appropriate; what is dangerous is the subtle assumption that schools' primary responsibility has shifted from instruction to mental health management.

Teaching children well is not in tension with caring for their wellbeing — it is itself an act of care, and the evidence most clearly shows that academic achievement, particularly literacy, is what changes life outcomes for the most vulnerable students.
quotes: The most powerful thing a school can give a child is an education. We have spent too long being distracted from it.
What I am questioning is something subtler and, I think, more dangerous: the slow drift away from the belief that teaching children well is itself a profound act of care.

When we load schools with the expectation that their primary responsibility is emotional regulation, therapeutic support, and wellbeing management, we risk quietly deprioritising the thing that schools are uniquely positioned to do. And the thing that the evidence most clearly suggests changes life trajectories for disadvantaged children.

The Grattan Institute's 2024 report, The Reading Guarantee, confirmed what many of us already knew: in a typical Australian classroom of 24 students, eight cannot read proficiently. One in three children not reading proficiently largely because they have not been taught effectively enough.

The report pointed directly at two approaches being implemented in Australian classrooms: the whole-language model, popular since the 1970s and based on the idea that reading is a natural, unconscious process, and balanced literacy, which the report described as 'contrary to scientific evidence.'

Having taught in and led curriculum and instructional improvement in underprivileged schools, I know what it looks like when a child walks through the school gate carrying the weight of things no child should have to carry. I know what it asks of teachers and leaders.
